input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

output:
The following discussion summarizes conceptual limitations and observed failure modes of the graph-aware prompting workflow. Because no external retrieval excerpts or experimental artifacts are attached to this draft, the items below are presented as general background knowledge and methodological caveats rather than empirically validated claims.

- Dataset scale and curation constraints (general background knowledge): The quality of section-level evidence injection depends on the size, topical coverage, and curation of the underlying corpus. Limited or narrowly curated corpora can leave some sections without high-quality supporting documents, forcing the generator to rely on weaker or more tangential evidence. In practice this can increase the rate of unsupported assertions and reduce the usefulness of automatic citation guidance.

- Domain transfer and topical coverage risks (general background knowledge): A document graph and retrieval strategy tuned for a particular domain may not generalize to different research areas. Domain-specific terminology, citation practices, and typical evidence types (e.g., datasets vs. theory papers) can produce mismatches between retrieved items and the claims expected in a section. Such mismatches can manifest as poorly matched citations, omission of canonical references, or generation that omits required methodological detail.

- Dependence on retrieval quality and provenance (general background knowledge): The pipeline’s reliance on retrieval and ranking creates a single point of failure: omissions, index errors, or low-quality ranking can propagate into section text. If the retrieval stage returns partially relevant or incorrect documents, evidence-aware prompts may include misleading provenance, and the constrained JSON output will still reflect the injected (but weak) sources unless additional validation is performed.

- Citation mismatch and propagated errors across the graph (general background knowledge): The section graph encodes dependencies that cause upstream errors to affect downstream sections. For example, an incorrect or weakly supported claim in an early (leaf) section can be cited by multiple parent sections during assembly, amplifying an initial mistake. Automated assembly and bibliography generation therefore require conservative rules and checks to avoid propagating a single erroneous citation widely through the manuscript.

- Runtime, cost, and human-in-the-loop editing tradeoffs (general background knowledge): Graph construction, per-section retrieval, and JSON-constrained generation introduce additional computational and human-review overhead relative to simple linear prompting. These costs affect iteration speed and may limit practical use for rapid drafting. Moreover, strict schema validation can produce failure modes where automatic repair attempts either over-correct or produce terse outputs that require manual expansion.

- Evaluation and audit limitations (general background knowledge): Assessing hallucination rates and citation fidelity requires careful annotation and provenance tracing. Without comprehensive, domain-representative datasets and standardized annotation protocols, reported improvements may reflect dataset idiosyncrasies or annotation biases rather than general algorithmic gains. Reproducible audits depend on saving full retrieval traces, intermediate JSON outputs, and generated bibliography files.

Mitigations and recommended practices (general background knowledge):
- Treat retrieval and ranking as first-class citizens: invest in corpus expansion, domain-specific indexing, and provenance logging so that each injected citation can be traced to a concrete document and retrieval score.
- Use conservative validation heuristics: require explicit evidence for normative factual claims and flag unsupported assertions for human review rather than attempting aggressive automatic repair.
- Limit propagation risk: when assembling parent sections, prefer local re-retrieval or re-validation of cited items instead of blindly reusing upstream citations.
- Design the human-in-the-loop workflow to support fast edits: expose machine-readable JSON and retrieval traces to editors, and provide lightweight interfaces for approving, replacing, or annotating citations.

Finally, we emphasize that these limitations are presented as conceptual caveats for the proposed workflow. Empirical quantification of their prevalence and impact requires systematic experiments and curated annotation protocols, which are outside the scope of this section.
